# Designing Precise and Consistent Piezoelectric Vibration Isolation Systems

Accuracy is improved most reliably by treating the isolator as one electromechanical measurement-and-control system. Hardware must provide low-noise, correctly mounted sensors; actuators and amplifiers must supply predictable force over the required stroke and bandwidth; the structure must place modes, stiffness, preload, and thermal paths under control; and algorithms must combine feedback robustness with model-based compensation. Consistent products require the same discipline across the lifecycle: measurable requirements and allocated tolerances in design, followed by controlled suppliers, standardized assembly, product-specific calibration, traceability, statistical process control, and system-level end-of-line testing in production.

The key practical conclusion is that nominally identical parts are not automatically identical isolators. Piezoelectric coefficients, capacitance, stiffness, bonding, preload, alignment, sensor phase, and structural modes can vary enough that each completed assembly needs characterization. A common mechanical and electronic design should therefore be combined with controlled unit-specific calibration data and a released production process.

This report first defines the architecture, accuracy dimensions, and error mechanisms. It then examines hardware, structure, manufacturing, and control algorithms before distinguishing the management controls required during design transfer from those required during serial production.

## 1. System architecture, accuracy metrics, and error sources

### 1.1 Roles and interfaces in the closed loop

A precision piezoelectric vibration isolation system has three functional paths:

1. A sensing path measures the disturbance, the payload response, the relative motion between payload and base, or the force carried by an isolator.

2. A control path converts those measurements into actuator commands, normally using feedback, feedforward, or both.

3. A force-and-motion path converts the electrical command into piezoelectric strain, actuator force, structural deformation, and finally payload motion.

Active vibration control is commonly described in exactly these terms: a sensor measures external or floor vibration and an actuator produces a counterforce. [Beijen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/acc.2015.7171051) describe this as the basic active-vibration-control path for precision equipment.

A representative base-isolation system contains a floor or base, an isolator structure, a payload or inertia block, sensors, piezoelectric actuators, power amplifiers, and a real-time controller. Let $`d`$ denote a base or internal disturbance, $`y`$ the payload motion, $`u`$ the actuator command, and $`n`$ measurement noise. A simplified signal model is:

```math
y(s)=G_d(s)d(s)+G_u(s)u(s)
```

```math
y_m(s)=H(s)y(s)+n(s)
```

Here, $`G_d`$ is the disturbance-to-payload transfer function, $`G_u`$ is the actuator-to-payload transfer function, and $`H`$ includes sensor dynamics, mounting effects, signal conditioning, conversion, and timing delay. The controller uses $`y_m`$, and possibly a measured disturbance reference $`d_m`$, to calculate $`u`$.

The sensor is therefore not merely an accessory to the controller. Its location, orientation, mass, bandwidth, phase, noise, and connection stiffness become part of $`H(s)`$. Likewise, the actuator is not just a force source: its capacitance, voltage-to-force gain, hysteresis, creep, preload, stiffness, resonances, and amplifier delay become part of $`G_u(s)`$.

The inverse piezoelectric effect provides the actuator’s basic operating principle: an applied electric potential produces mechanical strain and precision motion. A practical electromechanical model passes a control voltage through a linear amplifier, represents the piezoelectric element as an electrical capacitance and electromechanical force source, and then maps that force through mass, damping, and stiffness to displacement. [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) review this coupled electrical, mechanical, hysteretic, and dynamic model.

### 1.2 What “accuracy” means in an isolation system

“Accuracy” has several distinct meanings. A system can have low residual acceleration but poor measurement calibration, or excellent static displacement repeatability but inadequate isolation at a structural resonance. Requirements should therefore name the metric, frequency range, operating condition, and measurement method.

| Accuracy dimension | Meaning | Typical measure |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation effectiveness | How much base or disturbance motion reaches the payload | Transmissibility $`T(f)=Y_{\mathrm{payload}}(f)/Y_{\mathrm{base}}(f)`$, often in dB |
| Residual motion | Remaining acceleration, velocity, displacement, or tilt | RMS, peak, spectral density, or integrated band value |
| Measurement fidelity | Whether a sensor reports the true motion or force | Noise density, sensitivity error, phase error, bias, cross-axis sensitivity |
| Dynamic accuracy | Ability to respond without excessive delay or distortion | Bandwidth, latency, settling time, overshoot, gain margin, phase margin |
| Nonlinear accuracy | Error caused by history, amplitude, time, or load | Hysteresis, creep, nonlinearity, saturation, drift |
| Repeatability and reproducibility | Variation within one unit, between units, operators, or lots | Standard deviation, range, capability indices, uncertainty |
| Long-term stability | Retention of performance under temperature, humidity, cycling, and aging | Drift, modal shift, calibration change, fatigue or insulation degradation |

Isolation itself is frequency-dependent. A passive mass-spring system amplifies motion around resonance and attenuates above resonance. For an ideal undamped isolator, the high-frequency asymptote is approximately $`-40`$ dB per decade, while damping reduces resonance amplification at the cost of some high-frequency isolation. [Bartel et al.](https://past.isma-isaac.be/downloads/isma2014/papers/isma2014_0145.pdf) describe this passive-versus-active trade-off.

A practical illustration is given by Tjepkema, van Dijk, and Soemers: if floor motion is limited to $`3\ \mu\mathrm{m/s}`$ RMS on the VC-E curve and the selected isolation system has a $`1\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ corner frequency, the supported-machine acceleration can be calculated from the floor spectrum and the selected transmissibility curve. The result is conditional on that disturbance spectrum and transfer function, not a universal performance value. [Their evaluation](https://www.euspen.eu/knowledge-base/ICE11211.pdf) is useful because it links an accuracy claim to both the measured environment and the isolator’s frequency response.

### 1.3 The end-to-end error budget

An error budget should separate errors by physical origin and by whether they are random, systematic, or coupled.

| Error source | Mechanism | Typical consequence | Main countermeasure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensor noise and bias | Intrinsic electronics, seismic element, thermal noise, bias drift | False motion and noise injection into the loop | Select by noise density and range; filter and calibrate |
| Sensor mounting | Tilt, mass loading, soft adhesive, local structural mode | Gain or phase error; apparent cross-axis motion | Rigid, repeatable mounting and frequency-response verification |
| Cross-axis sensitivity | Sensor or actuator responds to other axes | Rotation or lateral motion appears in the controlled axis | Symmetric geometry, six-axis calibration, matrix decoupling |
| Signal chain | Cable motion, impedance mismatch, EMI, power-supply harmonics | Added noise, attenuation, phase shift | Impedance conversion, shielding, strain relief, grounding |
| ADC/DAC | Quantization, aperture jitter, saturation, anti-aliasing | Discrete command noise or amplitude error | Adequate ENOB, dynamic range, synchronized conversion |
| Actuator variation | $`d_{33}`$, stiffness, capacitance, resonance, hysteresis, creep | Unit-dependent force and stroke | Characterize each actuator or assembled module |
| Preload and alignment | Boundary conditions change actuator stiffness and output | Nonlinear gain, parasitic motion, premature failure | Measured preload, datums, fixtures, alignment inspection |
| Structure | Flexible interfaces, resonances, damping changes | Amplification, coupling, settling error | Modal design, stiffness balance, damping, cable isolation |
| Thermal and environmental effects | CTE mismatch, temperature-dependent coefficients, humidity, aging | Gain drift, mode shift, bias, bonding degradation | Material matching, thermal mapping, environmental qualification |
| Controller | Model error, delay, phase loss, saturation, adaptation instability | Residual vibration or instability | Robust design, deterministic timing, stability verification |
| Production variation | Part dimensions, bonding, torque, firmware or calibration mismatch | Unit-to-unit performance spread | Process capability, traceability, end-of-line screening |

The total error cannot be treated as one undifferentiated number. Independent random contributions can be combined approximately by root-sum-square methods, but systematic effects such as temperature gain drift, a repeatable phase lag, or a consistent cross-axis term should be measured and compensated rather than statistically hidden. Coupled effects need special care: a change in preload can alter piezoelectric hysteresis, structural stiffness, resonance, and controller stability simultaneously.

The effect of cross-coupling is clear in a six-degree-of-freedom model. [Nguyen et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/14/17/7966) distinguish diagonal transfer functions, which map an input force or torque into the same motion coordinate, from non-diagonal transfer functions representing internal interference. Isolation performance is therefore affected not only by external vibration but also by the plant’s own cross-axis dynamics.

### 1.4 Accuracy is defined by the installed system

Component specifications do not determine system accuracy by themselves. A sensor with excellent catalog noise can be mounted on a flexible bracket; an actuator with high blocked force can be connected through a compliant or thermally unstable interface; and a controller with high numerical resolution can be limited by sensor noise and delay.

A 2010 active-hard-mount investigation demonstrates this point. The concept maintained support stiffness about 300 times larger than typical soft mounts and reduced vibration by a factor of 20 to approximately $`1\ \mathrm{mm/s^2}`$ RMS in the reported tests. Yet the residual was not comparable with typical soft-mount performance because sensor noise and signal-conditioning delay dominated the remaining error. [The University of Twente thesis](https://doi.org/10.3990/1.9789036530163) therefore supports a general design rule: increasing actuator authority or structural stiffness does not compensate automatically for a poor measurement and timing path.

## 2. Hardware design for sensors, actuators, and controllers

### 2.1 Select sensors by controlled variable and disturbance spectrum

Sensor choice should begin with the variable that must be controlled, not with a preferred sensor technology. Acceleration, velocity, displacement, tilt, and force sensors observe different points in the loop and have different low-frequency and environmental limitations.

A useful comparison is:

| Sensor modality | Strengths | Main limitations | Good use in an isolator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inertial accelerometer | Direct absolute acceleration; compact; broad high-frequency response | Bias, gravity sensitivity, noise at very low frequency, mounting sensitivity | Payload or base acceleration feedback |
| Geophone or velocity sensor | Strong low-frequency velocity sensitivity; useful for floor motion | Limited displacement/DC information; frequency-dependent response | Floor-reference feedforward or hard-mount feedback |
| Capacitive displacement sensor | Non-contact relative displacement; good near-static information | Gap, contamination, temperature, cable, and alignment sensitivity | Payload-to-base relative motion or tilt measurement |
| Optical displacement/interferometric sensor | Very high displacement resolution; non-contact | Line of sight, reflectivity, alignment, cost, environmental sensitivity | Reference metrology, calibration, or high-resolution payload sensing |
| Force sensor or self-sensing piezo | Measures load-path force; can enable local force feedback | Force-loop dynamics, preload sensitivity, crosstalk, low-frequency limitations | Local actuator or isolator force control |

A sensor-selection study evaluated five devices for active isolation: the MMF KB12VD piezoelectric accelerometer, Colibrys SiFlex 1500 capacitive MEMS accelerometer, GeoSpace GS-11D geophone, Brüel & Kjær 8001 piezoelectric force sensor, and Lion Precision C5 capacitive displacement probe. It calculated each device’s noise spectrum and contribution to supported-machine acceleration. The study found that measured noise for three tested sensors agreed reasonably with theoretical estimates, differing by at most a factor of two when 50 Hz power-supply harmonics were excluded, and concluded that the analyzed system was principally limited by sensor fundamental noise rather than signal conditioning. [Tjepkema, van Dijk, and Soemers](https://www.euspen.eu/knowledge-base/ICE11211.pdf) provide this comparison, but it should not be read as a universal ranking: the best sensor depends on the required frequency band, range, payload mass, environmental conditions, and control architecture.

#### Accelerometers, geophones, and low-frequency measurement

For low-frequency isolation, the distinction between MEMS and piezoelectric/IEPE accelerometers is important. MEMS sensors can measure DC and near-DC acceleration, including gravity, but may have higher noise density. IEPE sensors generally offer lower noise but are AC-coupled through an internal impedance converter and signal conditioner.

A 2024 measurement study compared two MEMS accelerometers with an IEPE accelerometer. The listed IEPE device had $`500\ \mathrm{mV/g}`$ sensitivity and $`2.0\ \mu g/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}`$ noise density, while the two listed MEMS devices had $`15.0`$ and $`22.9\ \mu g/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}`$ noise densities. However, the IEPE response was not flat at very low frequency: at $`0.2\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, its amplitude fell by approximately $`5.5\%`$ to $`8.5\%`$ relative to $`1\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, and phase shift reached up to $`20^\circ`$. [The Metrology study](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8244/4/1/4) therefore emphasizes sensor-specific, frequency-dependent calibration rather than reliance on a nominal sensitivity.

The IEPE signal path must include the sensor, cable, constant-current bias, coupling capacitor, load resistor, anti-alias filter, and ADC. In the cited setup, a MOSFET impedance converter changed the sensor’s high-impedance output to a low-impedance signal, a $`13\ \mathrm{V}`$ bias was supplied, the lower cutoff was approximately $`0.1\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, and a 24-bit delta-sigma converter was used. The lower measurable frequency depends on both sensor and conditioner, not on the ADC resolution alone.

Geophones are useful when velocity is the natural controlled variable or when a reliable floor reference is required. The active-hard-mount thesis selected absolute-motion sensors for feedback damping and used measured floor vibration for feedforward compensation. Commercial hard-mount systems similarly use geophone-type inertial sensors directed toward the floor to measure vibration velocity and command piezoelectric counteraction. [TMC’s STACIS description](https://www.techmfg.com/products/stacis/stacisiii) is a product-specific example of this architecture.

#### Displacement and tilt sensors

Relative displacement sensors measure the motion that the isolator is intended to suppress, but their installation can alter the measured plant. A capacitive probe needs a stable gap, clean surfaces, and controlled cable capacitance. An optical sensor needs a stable line of sight and carefully controlled angular alignment. Both can be excellent for calibration and closed-loop position control, but either can become a source of drift if the bracket or target expands thermally.

In a 2-DOF piezoelectric platform, a KEYENCE LK-G10 laser sensor was mounted in line with each motion direction, with a stated measurement range of $`\pm1\ \mathrm{mm}`$ and $`10\ \mathrm{nm}`$ resolution. That arrangement illustrates two important practices: the measurement axis should coincide with the intended motion axis, and the reference target should move with the controlled stage rather than with an unrelated structure. [Zhao and Li](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi8080245) used the laser sensor for displacement characterization, not as proof that the same metrology would be adequate for every isolation product.

Tilt is often the hidden variable in precision equipment. A vertical-pendulum tiltmeter with a bridge-type capacitive transducer and piezoelectric servo actuator reduced a $`6.0131\ \mu\mathrm{rad}`$ input tilt to below $`0.0103\ \mu\mathrm{rad}`$, reported as approximately $`-27.67\ \mathrm{dB}`$, under the tested conditions. [Wang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11104526) used this result to demonstrate a tilt loop; the magnitude is a device-specific experimental result, not a general performance guarantee.

#### Force sensors and self-sensing

Force feedback is useful when the controlled quantity is the force transmitted through an isolator or when payload displacement is difficult to measure. It can provide a local loop around an actuator and its preload structure, but the force sensor sees the stiffness and damping of its mounting path. It can also be sensitive to temperature, cable forces, and preload drift.

Self-sensing piezoelectric elements combine actuation and sensing in one structure. In a smart piezo stack, pressure generates charge on sensing electrodes, which is converted by a charge amplifier into a voltage. However, actuator deformation can change the sensor thickness and generate opposite-polarity charge. [Chen and Li](https://www.uvm.edu/~wli17/Paper/06748972.pdf) identified this actuator–sensor crosstalk experimentally and showed that it reduces the charge measured for an external force. A self-sensing design must therefore separate drive feedthrough from mechanical response, characterize the crosstalk, and avoid assuming that a compact sensor is automatically an accurate sensor.

### 2.2 Mounting, orientation, and cable design

A sensor should be mounted on the rigid body whose motion matters, with its sensitive axis aligned to the controlled coordinate. The bracket’s first mode should be well outside the control band, and the mounting interface should not introduce an unmeasured compliant layer. The same principle applies to calibration: the reference sensor and device under test should experience the same motion.

Cables are mechanical components in a precision isolator. A cable that is too stiff can inject force, add damping, alter a mode, or bypass an isolation stage. A cable that moves against a surface can create triboelectric or friction-induced noise. In a low-frequency IEPE study, the sensors and measurement module were mounted on the same slide and the coaxial cable was routed horizontally to suppress relative movement and cable-friction effects. [The Metrology study](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8244/4/1/4) provides direct experimental support for treating cable routing as part of the measurement design.

The sensitivity of modes to utilities is also measurable at system scale. In a Stewart-platform isolation system, slightly tightening a cable shifted the first three modal frequencies to $`1.2`$, $`1.73`$, and $`2.9\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, higher than in the initial cable condition because the cable had become stiffer. [Fang et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11704038/) show why a modal test with production cable routing is more meaningful than a test of the bare structure.

### 2.3 Choose actuator architecture by force, stroke, and bandwidth

Piezoelectric actuators should be selected against the required blocked force, free stroke, loaded stroke, stiffness, capacitance, resonance, voltage, current, duty cycle, and environmental range.

| Actuator architecture | Stroke and force tendency | Advantages | Principal accuracy risks |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multilayer stack | Short stroke, high blocked force and stiffness | Compact, fast, strong, suitable for hard mounts | High capacitance, high-voltage drive current, hysteresis, preload sensitivity |
| Unimorph or bimorph | Larger deflection, lower force | Useful for bending and compliant motion | Lower load capacity, bending-mode sensitivity, thermal and bonding effects |
| Amplified stack | Greater stroke with moderate force | Extends stack travel through flexure leverage | Flexure parasitic motion, reduced stiffness, additional modes and stress |
| Flexure-integrated stack | Motion, guidance, and preload in one compliant structure | No backlash, controlled axes, potentially low part count | Geometry and machining errors directly alter gain, modes, preload, and cross-axis coupling |
| Stepping or stick-slip piezo actuator | Large travel through repeated steps | Long range and high resolution | Friction, backward motion, wear, contact-force variation, step inconsistency |

The actuator review by [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) summarizes the fundamental trade-off: cantilevered unimorph and bimorph devices provide more motion but less generated force, while multilayer stacks provide limited motion but high blocked force. Flexural amplification increases stack displacement while retaining only moderate force.

For a vibration isolator, the stack is often the preferred direct actuator because isolation requires force authority and high stiffness more than large free stroke. If displacement is insufficient, a flexure amplifier can be added, but its parasitic motion and lower natural frequency must be included in the plant model. A mechanism that looks advantageous in a static stroke calculation may reduce the usable control bandwidth.

The actuator should also be selected by ceramic behavior. A 2026 review compares soft PZT, which generally offers larger piezoelectric coefficients but more hysteresis and dielectric loss, with hard PZT, which generally offers lower loss, higher mechanical quality factor, and better high-frequency stability. The choice is application-dependent: a high-force, high-bandwidth isolator may favor lower-loss ceramic behavior, while a low-frequency large-stroke design may prioritize coefficient and travel. [Hua et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-1702/14/3/290) present this comparison in the context of non-resonant actuators; the same trade-off must be evaluated against the isolator’s actual frequency and duty cycle.

### 2.4 Design the high-voltage amplifier with the piezo load included

A piezo stack is primarily a capacitive load, with additional resistive, dielectric, cable, and amplifier effects. The reactive current is approximately proportional to capacitance and the rate of voltage change:

```math
i(t)\approx C_p\frac{dV(t)}{dt}+i_{\mathrm{leakage}}(t)
```

For a sinusoidal voltage of amplitude $`V_{\mathrm{pk}}`$ and frequency $`f`$, the capacitive current scales approximately as $`2\pi f C_p V_{\mathrm{pk}}`$. Consequently, an amplifier that is adequate at low frequency can current-limit, distort, or overheat at the upper end of the control band.

A high-voltage amplifier study modeled a stack as a capacitor of several microfarads in series with a resistance of several ohms and treated amplifier output resistance below $`1\ \Omega`$. It found that current increased with input frequency for fixed voltage amplitude and that stack capacitance and maximum operating frequency were critical driver parameters. [Xu et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/s20226528) also stress that amplifier stability must be analyzed and verified with the actual piezo stack connected as the load.

The amplifier design should therefore specify:

- output-voltage range and bipolar or unipolar operation;
- peak and continuous current;
- voltage slew rate;
- output impedance and cable inductance;
- load-dependent stability and phase response;
- voltage and current monitoring;
- protection against overvoltage, open circuit, short circuit, and depolarization;
- thermal behavior under the maximum duty cycle;
- electromagnetic compatibility with sensor wiring and ADC inputs.

A current limit is not only a reliability feature. If it is reached during a disturbance, the actuator command becomes nonlinear and the controller’s assumed plant changes. The current limit and voltage saturation must be included in disturbance-rejection simulations and acceptance tests.

### 2.5 Low-noise signal conditioning and dynamic range

The signal chain should preserve the weakest meaningful motion while tolerating the largest expected transient. That requires a dynamic-range budget from sensor output through conditioning, ADC, digital filtering, controller arithmetic, DAC, and amplifier.

A piezoelectric MEMS sensor example produced only about $`150\ \mu\mathrm{V}`$ for $`1\ \mathrm{m/s^2}`$ input from a $`30\ \mathrm{pF}`$ device. The circuit used a JFET common-source stage for high-to-low impedance conversion, an operational-amplifier gain stage, and filters for bandwidth definition and alias suppression. [The reported circuit study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8846575/) measured $`33\ \mathrm{dB}`$ gain and a $`-3\ \mathrm{dB}`$ cutoff near $`6\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ for its tested configuration.

The design implications are:

- use an input stage whose voltage and current noise are compatible with the sensor impedance;
- avoid loading a high-impedance piezoelectric source;
- place anti-alias filtering before the ADC;
- account for filter phase delay in the control loop;
- keep signal grounds and high-voltage return currents from sharing sensitive sensor paths;
- shield low-level signals from amplifier switching and digital clocks;
- avoid unnecessary gain before large disturbances that could cause saturation;
- use separate monitoring paths when diagnostic bandwidth differs from control bandwidth.

The IEPE chain illustrates why a nominally high-resolution ADC does not remove analog limitations. Its lower cutoff is set by the coupling network and sensor, while the anti-alias filter determines the usable upper band. The complete transfer function must be calibrated, including gain and phase.

### 2.6 ADC, DAC, quantization, and synchronization

The ADC should be selected by effective number of bits, input range, noise spectral density, sampling rate, aperture jitter, channel matching, and latency—not only by nominal resolution. The DAC should be selected by output range, settling, monotonicity, update rate, and output noise.

In one active-isolation example, a 16-bit DAC generated an equivalent actuator force with a standard deviation of $`0.5\ \mathrm{mN}`$, and the resulting acceleration contribution was highest at high frequencies. [Tjepkema, van Dijk, and Soemers](https://www.euspen.eu/knowledge-base/ICE11211.pdf) used that value as an example of how command quantization can become a mechanical noise source. The numerical value is specific to that setup; the design principle is general.

A useful command-resolution check is to translate one DAC count through the amplifier gain, actuator force gain, structural transfer function, and payload mass. If the resulting residual motion is above the allowable noise floor, more DAC resolution, a smaller amplifier range, a charge-based interface, or a mechanical transmission ratio may be needed. Increasing bits without reducing the full-scale range may not improve effective resolution if analog noise dominates.

Sampling and actuator updates should be deterministic and synchronized across axes. Time skew between sensors can appear as false phase or cross-axis motion. In a multi-axis loop, all sampled channels should have known relative timing, and the timestamp or phase relationship should be part of the calibration record.

A 2026 FPGA–ADC study demonstrates the value of treating synchronization as a measurable subsystem. Its Kintex-7/AFE7225 platform reached sampling rates up to $`125\ \mathrm{MS/s}`$, reported interface timing uncertainty below $`10\ \mathrm{ps}`$ RMS, and maintained $`88`$–$`91\ \mathrm{dB}`$ SNR over a 12-hour, 1 MHz test. Its zero-error capture result was bounded by the test memory depth rather than being a direct measurement of the intrinsic bit-error rate. [The study](https://doi.org/10.3390/data11010023) is not a vibration-isolator test, but it provides a useful hardware-design precedent: clock phase, data alignment, lock monitoring, and long-term timing drift should be verified rather than assumed.

For an isolation controller, latency matters more than an impressive internal clock frequency. The total loop delay includes sensor dynamics, analog filters, ADC conversion, scheduling, digital computation, DAC update, amplifier response, and actuator mechanics. The delay should be measured from physical motion to physical counterforce and represented in the open-loop model.

### 2.7 Calibration and hardware compensation

Calibration should be layered:

1. Calibrate sensor sensitivity, bias, frequency response, phase, cross-axis terms, and temperature dependence.

2. Calibrate amplifier gain, offset, current measurement, DAC gain, and ADC channel matching.

3. Characterize actuator capacitance, force or displacement, resonance, hysteresis, creep, and preload dependence.

4. Identify the assembled mechanical plant, including modal frequencies, cross-coupling, and closed-loop response.

5. Store the resulting parameters with the product serial number and firmware configuration.

ISO 16063-11 specifies primary vibration calibration of rectilinear accelerometers by steady-state sinusoidal vibration and laser interferometry over $`1\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ to $`10\ \mathrm{kHz}`$, with a frequency-dependent dynamic range. [ISO 16063-11](https://www.iso.org/standard/24951.html) is relevant when primary traceability is needed. ISO 16063-21 specifies comparison calibration of rectilinear vibration transducers from $`0.4\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ to $`10\ \mathrm{kHz}`$, with expanded uncertainty evaluated from significant sources. [ISO 16063-21](https://www.iso.org/standard/27053.html) is often more practical for production and field comparison calibration.

Calibration must include the actual signal path. A PZT calibration-chain study identified six stages from active source to output voltage: source, Green’s function, theoretical displacement, instrumental response, amplification/bandpass, and voltage. Contact, sensor, cables, and A/D conversion were included in instrumental response. [The calibration study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10921-021-00799-1) found that boundary conditions changed the response near resonant and anti-resonant frequencies, demonstrating why a sensor certificate alone is insufficient for a mounted isolator.

## 3. Structural design for stiffness, modes, alignment, and stability

### 3.1 Choose the isolation topology before optimizing parts

The central structural decision is whether the system should be soft and passively isolating, hard and actively controlled, or hybrid.

| Topology | Structural characteristic | Main benefit | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soft passive mount | Low stiffness and low natural frequency | Isolation above resonance with little electronics | Resonance amplification, poor direct-disturbance response, leveling and settling difficulties |
| Hard active mount | High stiffness with piezoelectric counterforce | Payload support, leveling, fast settling, active damping and low-frequency cancellation | Requires low-noise sensing, force authority, low latency, and stable control |
| Hybrid active–passive mount | Passive compliance or damping plus active piezo correction | Reduces passive resonance while limiting required active force | More interfaces, nonlinearities, and configuration dependencies |
| Serial multi-stage system | Isolation stages arranged in series | Large attenuation and modularity | Intermediate modes, cumulative alignment and cable-interface problems |
| Parallel multi-DOF system | Multiple actuators and flexures support one platform | Compactness, high stiffness, coordinated motion | Cross-axis coupling and need for complete multi-axis metrology |

The conflict between low stiffness and high support stiffness is architecture-dependent. A passive isolator seeks a low natural frequency so the disturbance lies above resonance. A hard active isolator intentionally retains high stiffness and uses measured motion or force to suppress the response. The University of Twente thesis used high support stiffness to avoid soft-mount leveling and direct-disturbance problems while adding feedback damping and floor feedforward. Commercial STACIS systems make a similar product-level trade-off: their manufacturer describes more than $`100`$-times higher stiffness than conventional soft isolation and active attenuation beginning at sub-Hz frequencies. [The STACIS white paper](https://www.techmfg.com/learning/whitepapers/piezo-driven-active-vibration-control-pushes-limits) is manufacturer evidence and should be treated as application-specific rather than a universal comparison.

The choice should be made from:

- measured floor and internal disturbance spectra;
- payload mass, center of gravity, inertia, and load distribution;
- required axes and rotations;
- allowable payload motion and tilt;
- direct-disturbance and settling requirements;
- available actuator stroke and force;
- control bandwidth and latency;
- environmental range and utility constraints.

### 3.2 Stiffness, mass, and natural-frequency placement

For a first design estimate, a single-degree-of-freedom mode has natural frequency $`f_n=(1/2\pi)\sqrt{k/m}`$. The actual system must then be analyzed with all relevant masses, flexure stiffnesses, actuator stiffness, preload, damping, and boundary conditions.

A heavy inertia block can reduce translational and rocking response. One practical design guide recommends an inertia block three to ten times the supported-equipment mass as a starting range, because added mass lowers natural frequency for a given isolator stiffness and lowers the center of gravity. [AMD Machines](https://amdmachines.com/blog/vibration-and-shock-isolation-for-precision-equipment/) presents this as practical guidance, not a product-independent law. The correct ratio must be verified against floor loading, payload inertia, structural modes, installation constraints, and actuator authority.

Modes should be placed deliberately:

- passive isolation modes should be below the dominant disturbance band when feasible;
- suspension and rocking modes should be separated from each other where possible;
- structural modes should be above the intended control band or explicitly included in the controller;
- actuator resonances should not lie inside a high-gain loop without damping or notch treatment;
- sensor-bracket modes should not be mistaken for payload modes;
- thermal and payload changes should not move a mode into the control crossover.

The goal is not simply to maximize every natural frequency. A very stiff structure may transfer more high-frequency force, reduce passive isolation, and demand greater actuator force. A very soft structure may offer low-frequency passive isolation but become difficult to level, susceptible to rocking, or slow to settle.

### 3.3 Damping and active damping

Passive damping lowers resonance amplification and helps prevent large transient motion, but it generally reduces the asymptotic isolation performance above resonance. Active damping can add damping selectively around a resonance while preserving a high-frequency isolation path.

Velocity feedback is a common active-damping mechanism. An inertial sensor estimates absolute payload velocity, and the controller commands an opposing force. Force feedback can damp a local mode but may be sensitive to actuator and load-path dynamics. Displacement feedback can control relative position and leveling but may inject structural modes if the sensor is mounted on a flexible bracket.

The active-hard-mount work found absolute-motion sensors preferable to force and displacement sensors for damping suspension and structural modes. Its experimental residual performance was limited by sensor noise and signal-conditioning delay, showing that active damping is constrained by the quality of the measurement path, not only by the chosen feedback law. [University of Twente](https://doi.org/10.3990/1.9789036530163).

A local force-feedback arrangement can nevertheless be useful. In an active–passive piezoelectric structure, disturbance passes through a passive element to a force sensor; the measured residual force forms the primary path, while a piezoelectric actuator compensates it through a secondary path. [The 2021 active–passive study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) used this architecture with an adaptive regulator.

### 3.4 Flexures, joints, and monolithic structures

Flexures are attractive because they provide motion without friction, backlash, lubrication, or rolling-contact variability. Their precision comes from elastic deformation, so their stiffness distribution, stress, machining accuracy, fatigue life, and parasitic compliance must be designed together.

A 2-DOF platform study compared right-angle, right-circle, and Z-shaped flexure hinges. At a $`10\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ applied displacement and $`100\ \mathrm{V}`$ drive condition, the reported maximum stresses were $`10.9\ \mathrm{MPa}`$ for the right-angle hinge, $`46.5\ \mathrm{MPa}`$ for the right-circle hinge, and $`8.8\ \mathrm{MPa}`$ for the Z-shaped hinge. The Z-shaped hinge therefore had the lowest simulated stress in that geometry. However, the same platform showed undesired transverse $`z`$ and $`\theta_x`$ motion at high frequency because of the Z-shaped geometry. [Zhao and Li](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi8080245) illustrate the important trade-off: a flexure that improves stress or stroke may worsen parasitic motion or modal separation.

The same study replaced a conventional parallel-four-connecting-rod arrangement with parallel six-connecting-rod structures to increase stage stiffness and reduce coupling deformation. It fabricated the platform as an integrated structural-steel part using wire electrical discharge machining. The integrated construction reduces assembled interfaces, but it transfers accuracy requirements to the WEDM process, stress relief, inspection, and datum control.

A monolithic structure is not automatically more repeatable than an assembled structure. Its advantages are fewer joints, no screw preload variation at the moving mechanism, and potentially better geometric symmetry. Its disadvantages include:

- sensitivity to material residual stress and machining distortion;
- difficult inspection of internal flexure dimensions;
- limited repairability;
- higher tooling or WEDM cost;
- possible difficulty integrating sensors and preload adjusters.

An assembled structure can provide adjustability and easier replacement, but requires controlled datums, torque, bonding, preload, and alignment.

### 3.5 Serial and parallel architectures

Serial and parallel architectures have different coupling mechanisms.

A serial stage nests one motion stage inside another. Its motion axes can be naturally separated, and coupling may be small even with open-loop control, but the moving mass and accumulated compliance reduce dynamic performance. A parallel stage drives one platform through several simultaneous legs. It can be compact and dynamically stiff, but its geometric coupling requires direct metrology and a coordinate transformation.

The comparison in [Micromachines](https://doi.org/10.3390/mi8080245) reports that serial piezoelectric platforms can achieve small coupling errors even with open-loop control and are suitable where cost, simple control, and reliability matter more than maximum dynamic performance. Parallel platforms generally offer better dynamic performance and orthogonality but require high-resolution measurement in all motion directions and more complex control.

For an isolation system, parallel architecture is often preferable when six-degree-of-freedom control and high support stiffness are required. A cubic-hexapod study showed that, under small-strut-displacement and small-adjacent-axis-coupling assumptions, a multi-DOF Stewart platform can be transformed into six approximately independent single-DOF systems. [The active–passive hexapod study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) provides the mechanism, but the approximation must be checked against the actual payload, stroke, and cross-axis transfer matrix.

### 3.6 Preload is part of the plant

Piezoelectric ceramics are strong in compression but vulnerable to tensile stress. Preload protects the ceramic, maintains contact, and sets the actuator’s effective stiffness. It also changes the electromechanical response.

A preload mechanism for a high-speed vertical nanopositioner used a cavity $`0.35\ \mathrm{mm}`$ shorter than the piezo stack. The cavity tolerance was $`+0.00/-0.02\ \mathrm{mm}`$, the actuator length tolerance was $`\pm0.05\ \mathrm{mm}`$, and the resulting design-level preload range was $`13.8`$–$`19.3\ \mathrm{N}`$. The authors specified an assembly sequence and sliding-fit contact surfaces to prevent base rotation and unequal screw forces. [Yong](https://www.eng.newcastle.edu.au/~yy582/Papers/Yong2016_preload.pdf) shows how apparently modest dimensional variation becomes a large functional variation when a stack is installed in a short preload cavity.

Preload must therefore be designed as a measurable parameter. Suitable measures include:

- direct load-cell measurement during assembly;
- calibrated displacement of a compliant preload element;
- torque-controlled fasteners only when torque-to-force variation is adequately characterized;
- a defined preload settling or conditioning cycle;
- post-assembly verification of actuator capacitance, stiffness, resonance, and stroke.

The coupling is not merely mechanical. A 2025 force-dependent Prandtl–Ishlinskii study found that flexible-hinge motion changes preload, preload generates internal piezoelectric charge, and the resulting reverse voltage opposes the external drive. The effective actuator voltage therefore changes with position and preload. The force-dependent model reduced average maximum tracking error by $`13.30\%`$ and average RMS error by $`6.38\%`$ relative to a classical PI model across six preload levels from $`25`$ to $`150\ \mathrm{N}`$. [Wang et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2066-0825/14/8/411) provide this evidence for a flexible-hinge stage; the exact coefficients cannot be transferred to another product without identification.

### 3.7 Alignment and parasitic motion

Alignment errors create forces and moments that are often larger than the desired controlled motion. The design should:

- place actuator force lines through intended centers of stiffness and mass where possible;
- use symmetric actuator layouts to balance moments;
- control parallelism, flatness, and angular alignment at defined datums;
- separate translations from rotations through geometry and coordinate transforms;
- minimize gaps, backlash, friction, and uncontrolled contact;
- make alignment features inspectable and repeatable;
- use flexible cable and utility breakouts.

In multi-axis systems, the actuator-to-platform mapping should be characterized as a matrix rather than assumed to be diagonal. For example, a six-degree-of-freedom experimental isolator used eight voice-coil actuators and eleven geophones: eight measured top-platform velocity and three measured base velocity. Six force/torque commands were mapped into actuator forces through a right-inverse allocation matrix, while measured platform velocities were reconstructed into six controlled coordinates. [Nguyen et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/14/17/7966) show the scale of the sensing and actuation problem even before control design begins.

The structure should also be verified with utilities attached. Rigid pipes, conduits, cable trays, vacuum lines, and coolant hoses can form vibration short circuits around an isolator. Flexible sections, service loops, or defined breakout points are needed to preserve the designed isolation path. [AMD Machines](https://amdmachines.com/blog/vibration-and-shock-isolation-for-precision-equipment/) identifies rigid utilities as a direct bypass mechanism and notes that levelness may need to be maintained to approximately $`0.02\ \mathrm{mm/m}`$ or tighter in some precision installations.

### 3.8 Thermal stability, humidity, and damping

Temperature affects both sensors and the mechanical plant. A 2024 IEPE study found that a $`30^\circ\mathrm{C}`$ temperature change altered sensor frequency response and that, over $`-10^\circ\mathrm{C}`$ to $`+50^\circ\mathrm{C}`$, sensitivity deviation reached up to $`10\%`$ in the tested low-frequency range. The same study found that the first mode of an aluminum cantilever shifted from $`8.79\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ at $`20^\circ\mathrm{C}`$ to $`9.74\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ at $`-10^\circ\mathrm{C}`$ and $`8.39\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ at $`50^\circ\mathrm{C}`$. [The Metrology study](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8244/4/1/4) demonstrates that an apparent structural change can be a sensor change, a structural change, or both.

Humidity may be less influential over part of the frequency range when the sensor is hermetically sealed, but that cannot be generalized to exposed flexures, adhesives, cables, ceramic insulation, or the piezoelectric stack. The same study found up to a $`4\%`$ sensitivity change at $`0.2\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ between $`30\%`$ and $`80\%`$ relative humidity, while changes from $`0.3`$ to $`1.0\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ were not significant in that test.

A low-temperature piezoelectric-stack study measured a $`15\%`$–$`30\%`$ reduction in static load-bearing response from $`20^\circ\mathrm{C}`$ to $`-70^\circ\mathrm{C}`$, while increasing compressive prestress from $`0`$ to $`6\ \mathrm{MPa}`$ increased the static response by $`79\%`$–$`90\%`$. Dynamic capacity also degraded over the tested $`1`$–$`6\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ range. [Li et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/25/12/3642) measured one stack and one instrumented assembly, so these values are not universal design coefficients; they show why temperature and preload must be specified as operating conditions rather than treated as secondary tests.

Structural design responses include:

- matching coefficients of thermal expansion where possible;
- placing sensitive axes symmetrically around thermal centers;
- reducing thermal gradients rather than only controlling average temperature;
- separating warm amplifiers and digital electronics from the payload structure;
- using temperature sensors near the actuator, flexure, sensor, and payload;
- characterizing modal frequency and damping over temperature;
- mapping sensor gain and actuator force versus temperature;
- protecting ceramics, adhesives, electrodes, and insulation from humidity;
- using vacuum only when the resulting damping and thermal behavior are acceptable.

For a pendulum or flexure sensor, reducing air damping can expose internal material damping as the dominant thermal-noise mechanism. [The vertical-pendulum study](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11104526) makes this distinction explicitly. Vacuum, therefore, is not a universal noise solution; it changes which loss mechanisms must be controlled.

## 4. Manufacturing processes, calibration, and metrology

### 4.1 Control piezoelectric material and actuator-process variation

Piezoelectric performance begins with ceramic composition, powder preparation, binder content, forming, electrode deposition, burnout, sintering, machining, poling, encapsulation, and aging. Each operation can change dielectric loss, capacitance, stiffness, $`d_{33}`$, polarization, resonance, insulation, fatigue, and temperature dependence.

A manufacturer’s process description for bulk piezoceramics includes mixing and ball milling, heating, binder burnout at $`750^\circ\mathrm{C}`$, sintering at $`1250`$–$`1350^\circ\mathrm{C}`$, machining, metallization, and high-field poling in a heated oil bath. Its thin-film multilayer route uses foil casting down to $`20\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ and co-firing below $`1100^\circ\mathrm{C}`$. The manufacturer states that heating and sintering cycles require tight tolerances because small changes affect material quality and properties, and reports final testing of material and components. [PI Ceramic](https://www.pi-usa.us/en/products/piezo-flexure-nanopositioners/piezo-motion-control-tutorial/tutorial-4-16) provides these process details.

The most important manufacturing implication is that a nominal material coefficient is not a sufficient acceptance criterion for a finished stack. The same source notes that piezoelectric coefficients vary with temperature, pressure, electric field, form factor, and mechanical and electrical boundary conditions. It specifically states that preloaded stacks and lever-amplified systems cannot be described sufficiently by small-signal material parameters, so stiffness, load capacity, displacement, and resonant frequency should be measured on the individual component or system.

Material and supplier controls should include:

- approved ceramic formulation and powder source;
- incoming chemical, particle-size, moisture, and lot documentation;
- controlled binder and solvent formulations;
- sintering profile, furnace calibration, atmosphere, and loading records;
- electrode thickness, continuity, adhesion, and resistance;
- poling field, temperature, duration, and orientation;
- capacitance, dielectric loss, insulation, and polarization checks;
- d33 or equivalent material sampling;
- lot identification retained through assembly;
- formal review before any material, electrode, encapsulation, or process substitution.

A 2026 multilayer lead-free piezoceramic study provides an example of process inspection: tape casting produced eleven piezoceramic layers, and microscopy, SEM, and EDS were used to verify layer thickness and ceramic–electrode contact. Its measured device had approximately $`53\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ ceramic layers and $`3\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ internal electrodes. [The Nature Communications study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72278-y) is a material-development example rather than a production-control standard, but it illustrates the need to inspect internal layers rather than rely only on exterior dimensions.

### 4.2 Control machining and dimensional tolerances

Machining tolerances should be allocated from functional sensitivity, not from what a machine can nominally produce. Critical dimensions include:

- flexure thickness and hinge radius;
- actuator cavity length and parallelism;
- preload-element geometry;
- sensor and actuator datum locations;
- platform flatness and perpendicularity;
- alignment-pin locations;
- cable and utility breakout positions;
- bond-line recesses and contact surfaces.

A sensitivity model can be expressed locally as:

```math
\Delta y\approx\sum_i\frac{\partial y}{\partial p_i}\Delta p_i
```

where $`p_i`$ are part, material, or assembly parameters and $`y`$ is a system characteristic such as preload, modal frequency, actuator gain, or cross-axis error. The terms with the largest product of sensitivity and variation deserve tighter tolerance, better inspection, or a design change.

Wire EDM is useful for monolithic flexures because it can produce complex compliant geometries without assembled joints. The 2-DOF platform cited earlier used WEDM to create an integrated steel structure. However, WEDM accuracy must be evaluated together with wire compensation, taper, residual stress, heat-affected effects, surface finish, and post-machining distortion. A monolithic flexure should be inspected by coordinate measurement, optical measurement, or functional stiffness testing rather than by checking only overall length and width.

The preload example from [Yong](https://www.eng.newcastle.edu.au/~yy582/Papers/Yong2016_preload.pdf) demonstrates tolerance propagation. A $`+0.00/-0.02\ \mathrm{mm}`$ cavity tolerance and $`\pm0.05\ \mathrm{mm}`$ actuator-length tolerance produced a calculated preload range of $`13.8`$–$`19.3\ \mathrm{N}`$. That range is a design-level calculation, not a statistical distribution, but it identifies the correct question for production: what measured preload distribution results after actual machining and assembly?

### 4.3 Standardize bonding, assembly, and alignment

Bonding can change stiffness, damping, thermal expansion, creep, and resonance. The process should specify:

- adhesive type, batch, storage, and working life;
- surface preparation and cleanliness;
- bond-line thickness and volume;
- dispensing equipment and calibration;
- fixture geometry and clamping force;
- cure time, temperature, humidity, and post-cure;
- inspection for voids, squeeze-out, delamination, and contamination;
- acceptance criteria for the cured joint.

The bonding thermal budget is especially important for thin-film and multilayer piezoelectric devices. A wafer-level PZT process compared electrode systems after thermal treatment, selected Cr/Au because it caused the least degradation, protected the electrode with $`\mathrm{Al_2O_3}`$, and used low-thermal-budget parylene bonding. The fabricated devices retained $`85.91\%`$ of pristine remanent polarization and $`94.30\%`$ of saturation polarization; elevated temperature caused more severe degradation. [The IOP study](https://beta.iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6382/ae4b4a/pdf) supports controlling thermal exposure and bonding chemistry, although its MEMS process is not a complete isolation-assembly process.

Assembly instructions should define the sequence and the reference datums. A robust sequence commonly seats the structure against hard locating features, installs the actuator without side loading, establishes preload through a compliant or measured element, and tightens fasteners in a specified order. The Yong preload design secured top screws before bottom horizontal screws and used sliding-fit contact surfaces to avoid base rotation and unequal horizontal installation forces.

Fixtures should make incorrect assembly difficult. Useful features include:

- asymmetric locating pins to prevent reversed installation;
- hard datums that do not rely on adhesive position;
- preload stops or load-cell feedback;
- alignment targets for optical or capacitive sensors;
- torque-controlled drivers with tool calibration;
- automatic recording of force, displacement, torque, and cure time;
- replaceable wear components with life limits;
- protected cable routing and strain relief.

An assembly that requires an expert to “feel” the correct preload or alignment is not ready for consistent production.

### 4.4 Measure the completed actuator and isolator

Component inspection is necessary but not sufficient. The finished assembly should be tested under controlled loading and boundary conditions.

At the actuator level, useful measurements include:

- capacitance and dielectric loss;
- insulation resistance and leakage;
- free stroke versus voltage;
- blocked force or force–displacement curve;
- stiffness;
- resonance frequency and damping;
- hysteresis loop at defined amplitude and frequency;
- creep after defined voltage steps;
- temperature-dependent response;
- fatigue or cycle stability where relevant.

At the assembly level, add:

- preload;
- alignment and platform level;
- modal frequencies and mode shapes;
- cross-axis sensitivity;
- cable and utility influence;
- sensor gain and phase;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- residual acceleration, velocity, displacement, and tilt;
- amplifier current and voltage under representative disturbances.

The manufacturer guidance in [PI Ceramic](https://www.pi-usa.us/en/products/piezo-flexure-nanopositioners/piezo-motion-control-tutorial/tutorial-4-16) explicitly argues for individual characterization because material coefficients do not describe preloaded or amplified systems adequately. The resulting calibration record should not be treated as an optional service document; it is part of the product configuration.

### 4.5 Calibration traceability and measurement-system analysis

Sensor calibration should be traceable to a reference and performed over the actual frequency and environmental range. ISO 16063-21 comparison calibration couples a reference transducer and device under test to the same shaker motion, then calculates sensitivity and phase from their electrical outputs. [ISO 16063-21](https://www.iso.org/standard/27053.html) permits uncertainty evaluation from significant sources, including check-standard results.

A back-to-back calibration arrangement should control:

- common mechanical mounting;
- axis orientation;
- preload and torque;
- cable routing;
- shaker amplitude and frequency;
- temperature and humidity;
- reference calibration status;
- phase and amplitude processing;
- repeat measurements and uncertainty.

A 2025 reference-comparison calibration used a common sensor platform, sinusoidal acceleration from $`10`$ to $`1000\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, $`0.1`$–$`1g`$, $`25\pm1^\circ\mathrm{C}`$, and ten-cycle averaging at each point. It reported expanded uncertainty increasing from $`1.7\%`$ at $`10\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ to $`2.1\%`$ at $`1000\ \mathrm{Hz}`$, with reference calibration, environmental factors, and repeatability contributing approximately $`60\%`$, $`25\%`$, and $`15\%`$, respectively, at one reported operating point. [The Vibroengineering calibration study](https://doi.org/10.21595/vp.2025.25675) illustrates how an uncertainty budget should identify the dominant contributors instead of reporting only a single accuracy number.

Measurement-system analysis must distinguish:

- repeatability: variation when the same instrument, operator, part, and method are repeated;
- reproducibility: variation due to operators, setups, environments, and time;
- part variation: real unit-to-unit variation.

[Hoffa and Laux](https://dr.lib.iastate.edu/bitstreams/c3a8d337-b12f-4a40-aa68-3f1ff9adc0ff/download) report the AIAG P/T convention that a measurement system below $`10\%`$ is generally acceptable, $`10\%`$–$`30\%`$ may be acceptable depending on application importance and cost, and above $`30\%`$ is unacceptable. These are decision boundaries, not a substitute for engineering judgment. A measurement system that cannot resolve the isolator’s critical variation cannot support a meaningful capability study.

### 4.6 Process capability and inspection strategy

For a stable, approximately normal process with upper and lower specification limits, the common capability indices are:

```math
C_p=\frac{USL-LSL}{6\sigma}
```

```math
C_{pk}=\min\left(\frac{USL-\mu}{3\sigma},\frac{\mu-LSL}{3\sigma}\right)
```

$`C_p`$ measures potential spread if centered; $`C_{pk}`$ also reflects centering. Ppk includes longer-term variation and should not be confused with short-term Cpk. Capability indices are invalid or misleading when the measurement system is poor, the process is unstable, the sample is unrepresentative, or the specification does not describe the true functional requirement.

A worked production example in an APQP guide used 100 consecutive pilot-line samples for a force constant. The example reported $`C_p=1.67`$, $`C_{pk}=1.62`$, and an ongoing Cpk criterion of at least $`1.33`$, while distinguishing an initial Ppk criterion of $`1.67`$. It also recommended X-bar/R monitoring and reaction rules for nonrandom trends. [The APQP example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/) concerns a micro-actuator production flow, not a completed vibration isolator. Its value here is the structure of the method, not the transfer of its numerical capability to another product.

For an isolator, capability studies should target characteristics such as:

- actuator capacitance and resonance;
- flexure thickness and stiffness;
- preload;
- sensor sensitivity and phase;
- assembled natural frequencies;
- cross-axis response;
- amplifier gain and current;
- residual noise;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- settling time and control effort.

Critical characteristics should be measured on every unit when practical. Sampling can be used for destructive, expensive, or long-duration tests, but sampled qualification does not replace 100% screening of characteristics that can escape and materially affect isolation.

### 4.7 Evidence limits for product-specific manufacturing statistics

The supplied evidence supports the processes, mechanisms, and measurement methods above, but it does not provide a complete product-specific statistical record for a serial precision piezoelectric vibration isolator. Specifically unavailable are:

- lot-to-lot statistics for ceramic coefficients, actuator properties, bonding, and preload in completed isolator assemblies;
- a complete assembled-isolator Cp/Cpk/SPC study;
- target-product environmental and aging validation across production lots;
- product-specific supplier incoming-acceptance data and material-lot records;
- standardized-work and control-plan evidence for a complete isolator build;
- unit-to-unit distributions for system transmissibility, noise, modal response, and control performance.

The strongest supported conclusion is therefore procedural: these quantities must be defined as production evidence, measured with a capable measurement system, and linked to serial numbers. A component-level capability example cannot be presented as proof of complete isolator consistency.

## 5. Control algorithms and nonlinear-error compensation

### 5.1 Begin with a measured plant

Control design should begin with system identification of the assembled structure and its actual electronics. The model should include:

- actuator voltage-to-force or charge-to-force behavior;
- sensor gain, phase, and filtering;
- payload and inertia-block mass properties;
- flexure and mount stiffness;
- damping and structural modes;
- cross-axis transfer functions;
- preload and load dependence;
- temperature dependence;
- ADC/DAC delay and computation latency;
- saturation and current limits.

A useful sequence is to identify the open-loop frequency response at low amplitude, verify modes and cross-coupling, identify nonlinear response at representative voltage and preload, then design and test the controller. Identification should be repeated at significant payload, temperature, and operating-point corners.

### 5.2 Feedback, feedforward, and hybrid control

The major alternatives can be compared as follows:

| Architecture | Required information | Main strength | Main limitation | Appropriate use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Feedback | Payload, relative, force, or inertial response | Rejects disturbances and model uncertainty | Limited by sensor noise, delay, phase margin, and actuator authority | General-purpose isolation and active damping |
| Feedforward | Coherent disturbance reference, such as floor acceleration | Can cancel disturbance before it appears in payload response | Requires an accurate, causal reference and plant model | Measured floor vibration or periodic machinery disturbance |
| Hybrid feedback/feedforward | Both response and disturbance measurements | Combines model-based rejection with robustness | More sensors, calibration, computation, and failure modes | High-performance active isolation |
| Robust feedback | Plant uncertainty bounds and measured response | Guarantees bounded performance across modeled uncertainty | Conservative weighting and control effort | Variable payloads, cross-coupled multi-axis systems |
| Adaptive control | Online error or plant information | Tracks changing payload, temperature, and modes | Stability, convergence, excitation, and validation are harder | Slowly varying operating conditions or degradation |

Feedback remains the foundation because it does not require a perfect disturbance reference. The 2021 active–passive isolation study explains that feedforward uses a vibration-source reference, while feedback detects residual vibration without needing that reference. It also notes that feedforward generally requires more sensors, which can reduce weight and reliability. [The study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) therefore recommends selecting feedback when the disturbance reference is unreliable or expensive to obtain.

Feedforward is valuable when the reference is measured upstream of the payload and is sufficiently coherent with the disturbance. In the active-hard-mount thesis, measured floor vibration was used with adaptive filtered-x least-mean-square compensation. The standard FIR representation required many parameters, while a fixed-pole IIR representation achieved similar performance with fewer parameters and lower computation. Its performance depended critically on the selected fixed poles. [University of Twente](https://doi.org/10.3990/1.9789036530163).

A hybrid loop is often the practical choice: feedforward removes predictable, coherent disturbance components, while feedback stabilizes the plant and corrects model error. The hybrid controller comparison reported three techniques—filtered-x LMS feedforward, LQG feedback, and a combined feedforward-feedback structure—and proposed the hybrid for robust performance and fast convergence. [JSME International Journal](https://doi.org/10.1299/jsmeintmovic.6.1.105).

### 5.3 Active damping and disturbance rejection

Active damping should target the modes that matter to payload accuracy. A velocity-feedback loop can emulate a virtual damper; a force loop can suppress the transmitted force; and a relative-displacement loop can regulate leveling and low-frequency motion. The loop should be placed around the physical quantity that is both observable and causally controllable.

For low-frequency disturbance rejection:

- use absolute inertial sensing when base motion and structural modes are the principal concern;
- use relative displacement sensing when payload-to-base position or tilt must be maintained;
- use force sensing when the transmitted force is the critical output;
- use multiple sensors when rotations and cross-axis motion cannot be inferred reliably from one channel;
- avoid integrating noisy acceleration indefinitely without bias management;
- use high-pass or bias-estimation strategies to prevent integral drift.

A spacecraft isolation study combined a geophone for absolute velocity with a force sensor and used integral force feedback to suppress a hyperelastic resonance peak. It maintained a loaded natural-frequency target of $`15`$–$`25\ \mathrm{Hz}`$. In its uncompensated loop, phase margin was only $`1^\circ`$; a lead compensator increased it to $`17^\circ`$. [The spacecraft isolation study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10813719/) is a useful warning that an apparently responsive loop can be unstable or unusable until phase margin is deliberately restored.

Disturbance observers can estimate the combined effect of unmodeled hysteresis, force variation, structural vibration, and external disturbance. They are attractive when a detailed physical model is too costly or changes with operating conditions. However, the observer bandwidth must not amplify sensor noise, and its uncertainty bounds must be tested against saturation and delay.

### 5.4 Robust and multi-axis control

For a multi-axis isolator, independent single-axis PID loops are adequate only when the off-diagonal plant terms are sufficiently small. Otherwise, a coordinate transformation, feedforward decoupling, or multivariable controller is required.

A six-degree-of-freedom AVIS study first used feedforward compensators based on modeled off-diagonal transfer functions to suppress mutual interference and then applied mixed-sensitivity $`H_\infty`$ feedback. Ground vibration, direct platform disturbance, and compensation error were treated as uncertainty. The design used diagonal feedback channels after decoupling and selected weighting functions from system characteristics. [Nguyen et al.](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/14/17/7966).

The robust-control choice should reflect uncertainty:

- LQG is useful when a linear state-space model and stochastic disturbance assumptions are credible;
- mixed-sensitivity $`H_\infty`$ is useful when tracking, disturbance rejection, sensor noise, and control effort need explicit frequency weighting;
- modal or notch control is useful when a small number of well-identified resonances dominate;
- decoupling feedforward is useful when cross-axis dynamics are stable and accurately identified;
- gain scheduling is useful when payload or temperature changes are repeatable and measurable.

Robust control is not a substitute for structural design. If a cable changes a mode by several hertz or preload moves actuator gain substantially, the uncertainty model must include those variations or the production process must reduce them.

### 5.5 Adaptive and predictive control

Adaptation is justified when the plant changes during normal operation and when a safe fixed controller cannot meet the full performance requirement. Possible changing variables include payload mass, payload center of gravity, temperature, actuator preload, ceramic aging, and damping.

Examples include:

- Youla-parameter adaptation with recursive least squares to suppress time-varying deterministic residual vibration;
- model-reference adaptive control with online parameter updates;
- adaptive filtered-x LMS for changing disturbance paths;
- fuzzy or ANFIS adaptation for nonlinear parameter dependence;
- sliding-mode predictive control with an observer for matched and mismatched disturbances;
- online modal or frequency-response estimation followed by bounded gain scheduling.

The adaptive Youla design in [the 2021 active–passive study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/11/8/3338) used an inner LQG controller to shape the loop near the natural frequency and recursive least squares to tune the free Youla parameter online. The study reports suppression of unknown, time-varying, low-frequency deterministic residual vibration, while noting that the central controller alone could not completely suppress that component.

A 2019 fractional-order robust model-reference adaptive controller adjusted parameters online using fractional proportional–integral adaptation laws and used only measurable plant input and output. Its reported experiments covered a $`20`$–$`500\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ band and compared favorably with traditional MRAC in control effort. [The Journal of Vibration and Control study](https://doi.org/10.1177/1077546319875260) provides an example, not a reason to select fractional-order control by default.

A 2025 study applied output-feedback sliding-mode predictive control to an active–passive piezoelectric isolator with variable-mass payloads. A neural-network state observer and generalized proportional-integral observer estimated matched and mismatched disturbances, while receding-horizon optimization used predicted sliding-state information. [Su et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/TIE.2025.3563717) show how advanced control can address changing payloads, but such an algorithm also increases verification, computational, and failure-containment requirements.

For a product, adaptation should have:

- bounded parameter ranges;
- a known initialization and calibration state;
- excitation limits that cannot damage the actuator;
- a fallback fixed controller;
- lockout conditions for sensor failure or loss of observability;
- logged parameters and adaptation history;
- a requalification plan when the algorithm or update law changes.

### 5.6 Hysteresis and creep compensation

Piezoelectric hysteresis is a memory-dependent difference between increasing and decreasing displacement at the same voltage. It depends on voltage history, amplitude, frequency, preload, temperature, and mechanical boundary conditions. Creep is a slower time-dependent displacement drift after a voltage change.

The 2023 review reports dynamic hysteresis errors of about $`15\%`$ in one synthesis of the literature, increasing to almost $`35\%`$ at higher drive frequency. The values span different actuators and conditions, so they are not a universal specification, but they establish why open-loop voltage control is insufficient for high accuracy. [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) distinguish rate-independent models for low-frequency behavior from rate-dependent models needed at higher frequency.

#### Charge control

Charge control regulates the charge or current supplied to the piezoelectric element instead of relying only on voltage. Because actuator capacitance changes with operating state, charge control can reduce hysteresis and creep.

The principal options are:

- series-capacitor insertion;
- current-controlled charge amplification;
- capacitor-based charge sensing;
- linear or nonlinear charge controllers;
- digital charge amplifiers.

Series-capacitor insertion reduces sensitivity to capacitance variation by a factor $`C/(C+C_p)`$, where $`C`$ is the inserted capacitor and $`C_p`$ the actuator capacitance. The same voltage-divider effect reduces the voltage available to the actuator and therefore reduces stroke unless a higher source voltage is provided. [Kanchan et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11060155) describe this direct trade-off.

Charge control is attractive when hysteresis reduction is more important than maximum stroke and when specialized current-sensing hardware is acceptable. It is less attractive when the actuator must operate over a large dynamic range, when low-frequency leakage causes charge drift, or when several axes require closely matched charge loops. Voltage control with model-based compensation is usually easier to productize across actuator types, but it requires calibration and model management.

#### Model-based voltage compensation

Common hysteresis models include:

- Bouc–Wen: differential, relatively convenient to implement, and suitable for rate-dependent behavior when extended;
- Prandtl–Ishlinskii: operator-based, useful for rate-independent or modified asymmetric behavior, with an inverse often convenient for feedforward;
- Preisach: flexible memory representation but more demanding identification and inversion;
- Duhem: differential representation with rate dependence;
- Maxwell–Slip: intuitive spring/friction representation but limited for some high-frequency behavior;
- neural or fuzzy models: flexible, but dependent on training data and validation boundaries.

The model should be selected by required frequency range, minor-loop behavior, asymmetry, computational budget, inverse availability, and parameter stability across temperature and preload. A model with a small fitting error in one open-loop sweep may fail in closed loop if it does not reproduce minor loops, rate effects, saturation, or preload dependence.

The 2021 vertical-pendulum isolator used separate polynomial fits for ascending and descending actuator curves, inverted those models, and combined them with a digital PID adjuster implemented on an FPGA. Its inner-loop model error was less than $`0.042\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ for the tested actuator under stable laboratory calibration. [Wang et al.](https://doi.org/10.3390/app11104526) show the value of a simple model when speed and implementation simplicity matter, but the result is specific to the tested NAC2023 actuator and calibration environment.

High-gain feedback can reduce residual hysteresis and creep without explicitly modeling them. In an AFM piezo scanner, high-gain feedback reduced a measured hysteresis error from $`6.29\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ to $`1.04\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$, an improvement of more than $`83\%`$, and reduced a 15-minute creep error from $`8.41\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ to $`0.37\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$. Further gain increase was limited by gain margin. [Leang and Devasia](http://www.kam.k.leang.com/academics/pubs/LeangKK_2002.pdf) provide these results for an AFM scanner, demonstrating the trade-off between nonlinear-error rejection and stability.

The most robust product architecture is often:

- feedforward inverse hysteresis compensation for the repeatable part;
- feedback for residual hysteresis, creep, disturbance, and unit variation;
- temperature and preload scheduling or compensation;
- individual actuator parameters stored by serial number.

### 5.7 Feedback–feedforward integration

A two-stage controller separates tasks:

1. Feedforward uses an identified plant and inverse nonlinear model to generate the approximate voltage or force needed for the desired motion or disturbance cancellation.

2. Feedback corrects model error, external disturbance, sensor bias, actuator variation, and drift.

[Leang and Devasia](http://www.kam.k.leang.com/academics/pubs/LeangKK_2002.pdf) proposed high-gain feedback for hysteresis and creep, followed by inversion-based feedforward for vibration at high scan rates. They emphasize that feedback provides robustness to model uncertainty while feedforward provides high-speed dynamic compensation.

For vibration isolation, the analogous arrangement is:

- feedforward from a floor accelerometer or geophone for coherent floor disturbance;
- feedback from payload inertial or relative-motion sensors for residual motion;
- active damping around structural modes;
- actuator hysteresis compensation inside the drive path;
- supervisory limits around voltage, current, travel, temperature, and sensor validity.

The feedforward path must be causal. [Beijen et al.](https://doi.org/10.1109/acc.2015.7171051) show that perfect disturbance cancellation is impossible in practice because compensation arrives late, plant inversion is imperfect, controllers are discrete, and sensor dynamics contribute residual error. The resulting frequency-domain waterbed effect means that improving rejection in one band can create sensitivity or control effort elsewhere.

### 5.8 Latency, phase margin, and implementation limits

Every filter and computation adds phase lag. A useful first-order approximation is that a pure delay $`\tau`$ contributes phase lag $`-\omega\tau`$, so the same delay becomes more damaging as crossover frequency rises.

The control design should budget:

- sensor and conditioner delay;
- ADC conversion and sample-and-hold;
- digital scheduling and execution;
- communication and buffering;
- DAC update;
- amplifier group delay;
- actuator and structural phase;
- anti-alias and reconstruction filters.

The CAVI prototype reported a $`700\ \mu\mathrm{s}`$ data-acquisition delay. It used phase-lead and phase-lag action, a $`0.25\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ high-pass pole to prevent drift, and a $`100\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ low-pass pole to limit high-frequency sensor-noise coupling. High-Q mechanical modes above $`100\ \mathrm{Hz}`$ required a notch filter, and the combination of delay, roll-off, and notch phase loss limited high-frequency control. [The CAVI study](https://beta.iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1361-6382/adf0e2) also notes that cryogenic mode shifts can require a different notch frequency and controller design.
