Controller verification should include gain and phase margins at each payload and temperature corner, sensor and actuator tolerances, latency variation, saturation, quantization, and loss of a sensor. The controller should be tested both with the nominal model and with measured worst-case plant variants.

## 6. Design-phase management for identical-product consistency

### 6.1 Convert needs into measurable requirements

Consistency begins before the first prototype. Customer or machine-level needs should be converted into a requirements specification with:

- controlled axes and rotations;
- payload mass, center of gravity, inertia, and load distribution;
- floor and internal disturbance spectra;
- residual acceleration, velocity, displacement, and tilt limits;
- frequency bands and transmissibility limits;
- settling time and allowable overshoot;
- sensor noise, phase, and cross-axis limits;
- actuator force, stroke, voltage, current, and temperature limits;
- operating, storage, transport, and humidity conditions;
- service life and cycle count;
- calibration and traceability requirements;
- acceptance statistics and measurement uncertainty.

A requirement such as “low vibration” is not testable. It should become something such as a residual acceleration spectral-density limit over a named band under a defined payload, temperature, floor spectrum, and control state. A requirement such as “identical behavior” should become a distribution of unit-level metrics, a maximum allowable spread, and a comparison method.

An APQP/QFD guide illustrates the conversion of a vague haptic requirement into measurable values: resonant frequency, peak acceleration, rise time, and specified verification instruments. Its numerical example is for a micro-actuator rather than an isolation system, but the requirement structure is directly transferable. [Chen’s APQP example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/) emphasizes that every requirement should name both a measurable value and a verification method.

### 6.2 Build a requirements and error-budget traceability matrix

Each system requirement should link to:

- a responsible subsystem;
- a physical parameter;
- a tolerance or uncertainty allocation;
- a verification method;
- a test condition;
- an acceptance limit;
- a design record;
- a production control.

For example:

| System requirement | Dominant contributors | Design allocation | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|
| Residual acceleration in a low-frequency band | Sensor noise, floor reference, structural resonance, loop delay | Sensor noise budget, modal placement, controller phase margin | Shaker or measured-floor transmissibility test |
| Payload tilt | Rotational stiffness, center-of-mass offset, sensor alignment, cable torque | Symmetric support, tilt sensor calibration, flexible utilities | Six-axis tilt and cross-axis test |
| Unit-to-unit closed-loop gain | Actuator force constant, preload, sensor gain, amplifier gain | Individual calibration and tolerance limits | EOL frequency-response and closed-loop test |
| Long-term drift | Ceramic aging, adhesive creep, temperature, electronics offset | Material/environmental design and compensation maps | Thermal, humidity, storage, and aging tests |
| Settling time | Structural damping, active damping, delay, saturation | Mode separation, deterministic control, current reserve | Step or load-disturbance test |

This matrix prevents a common failure: assigning a system-level accuracy requirement to a controller team while leaving the largest error source—such as preload or sensor mounting—unallocated.

### 6.3 Allocate tolerances by sensitivity and interaction

Tolerance allocation should be performed on a coupled electromechanical model. Relevant variables include:

- flexure dimensions and elastic modulus;
- actuator $`d_{33}`$, capacitance, stiffness, and resonance;
- preload and bond-line thickness;
- sensor gain, phase, and orientation;
- amplifier gain, current, and output impedance;
- ADC/DAC quantization and timing;
- payload mass and center of gravity;
- temperature and thermal gradients;
- cable stiffness and routing.

Use sensitivity analysis to identify which variables materially affect residual motion or stability. Then choose the least expensive effective control:

- tighten the part tolerance;
- redesign the geometry to reduce sensitivity;
- add an adjustment or datum;
- measure and calibrate the parameter;
- schedule controller parameters;
- accept the variation only if the error budget permits it.

Worst-case allocation is appropriate for safety or hard travel limits. Statistical allocation can be appropriate for random, controlled dimensions, but only after process distributions and correlations are known. A Monte Carlo result is not evidence of consistency until it is validated against measured production distributions.

Preload is an example of an interaction requiring coupled analysis. A tolerance that changes preload can change actuator gain, hysteresis, stiffness, resonance, and fatigue simultaneously. Treating preload as an independent scalar error will understate its effect.

### 6.4 Verify the design at component, subsystem, and system levels

A V-model is effective when each development level has a corresponding verification level. [Bartel et al.](https://past.isma-isaac.be/downloads/isma2014/papers/isma2014_0145.pdf) describe a requirements-driven sequence in which contract requirements define component demands, component designs are verified, integration tests check system properties, and final testing validates the whole system against the original requirements.

A suitable verification sequence is:

1. Verify material and actuator properties, including capacitance, insulation, stroke, force, resonance, hysteresis, creep, and temperature behavior.

2. Verify flexure geometry, stiffness, stress, fatigue margin, alignment, and parasitic motion.

3. Verify the amplifier and signal chain with representative capacitive loads and sensor impedances.

4. Verify sensor frequency response, noise, cross-axis response, mounting, and calibration uncertainty.

5. Verify actuator–structure subassemblies with measured preload and production-representative cables.

6. Identify the integrated plant and compare measured modes and transfer functions with the model.

7. Verify the controller in simulation, hardware-in-the-loop, and physical closed-loop tests.

8. Verify environmental corners, payload corners, disturbance corners, and fault conditions.

9. Validate the intended installed use with the actual tool or a representative payload and floor spectrum.

TMC’s product literature makes performance conditional on comparing site floor-vibration data with the tool’s floor-vibration criteria and confirming that the isolator transfer function provides the required isolation. [The STACIS installation guidance](https://www.gmp.ch/pdf/Datasheets/TMC/STACIS%20product%20brochureGMP.pdf) illustrates why design verification cannot stop at a laboratory shaker test with an arbitrary disturbance.

### 6.5 Freeze configuration across hardware, software, and calibration

A precision isolator has several configuration items:

- mechanical drawings and tolerances;
- material and surface-treatment specifications;
- actuator and sensor part numbers;
- amplifier schematic, PCB revision, and component values;
- ADC/DAC configuration;
- FPGA or DSP firmware;
- controller gains and filters;
- nonlinear-model parameters;
- temperature and preload compensation maps;
- calibration fixtures and procedures;
- acceptance-test software;
- serial-number database schema.

All must be revision-controlled. A change to a capacitor, adhesive, sensor cable, firmware timing, filter coefficient, or actuator supplier can change the closed-loop plant. Engineering change review should ask:

- Does the change alter a calibrated parameter?
- Does it change a mode, delay, gain, noise floor, or thermal path?
- Does it affect interchangeability?
- Does it require re-identification or requalification?
- Which existing production units are affected?
- Can units built before and after the change be compared under the same test?

Supplier guidance for piezoelectric OEM programs recommends that the NPI package contain revision references, critical dimensions, performance targets, inspection methods, validation records, pilot-release criteria, and controlled scale-up. It also warns that material substitutions, process changes, tooling refreshes, inspection changes, packaging, and logistics changes may require review and revalidation. [Yujie Piezoelectric](https://yujiepiezo.com/blog/component-supplier-innovation-partner-piezoelectric-transducer-manufacturer/) provides this design-transfer guidance.

### 6.6 Define a calibration strategy before design release

Calibration should not be added after the mechanical and control design is frozen. The design should provide:

- accessible calibration interfaces;
- known reference points and datums;
- sufficient actuator stroke for calibration excitation;
- safe fixtures for blocked-force or displacement tests;
- temperature and preload sensing;
- firmware support for calibration mode;
- nonvolatile storage for unit-specific parameters;
- versioned calibration files;
- recalibration and requalification criteria.

For a piezoelectric isolator, the most useful strategy is often a hybrid of common nominal parameters and individual measurements. Use common model structure and common control laws, but store per-unit values for:

- sensor gain and phase;
- actuator voltage-to-force or voltage-to-displacement gain;
- capacitance and leakage;
- resonance frequency and damping;
- preload;
- hysteresis and creep parameters;
- cross-axis matrix;
- temperature compensation coefficients;
- final closed-loop correction.

A closed-loop piezo system manufacturer states that each delivered system is calibrated for linearity and repeatability, that results are recorded in a calibration protocol, and that the control system must be calibrated with the specific actuator. [piezosystem jena](https://www.piezosystem.com/piezopedia/measurement-systems/) gives a product-level example of this principle and reports a $`0.037\%`$ nonlinearity example at a $`157\ \mu\mathrm{m}`$ position. The numerical result is product-specific; the configuration rule is broadly applicable.

### 6.7 Transfer the design through a controlled pilot

Design transfer should include:

- a released bill of material and approved supplier list;
- controlled drawings with critical-to-function dimensions;
- process flow diagram;
- PFMEA or equivalent risk analysis;
- control plan;
- assembly work instructions;
- calibrated fixtures and gauges;
- operator training;
- golden sample or reference unit;
- first-article and pilot-build records;
- measurement-system analysis;
- capability data from consecutive pilot units;
- software and calibration release package;
- packaging and transport requirements;
- defined production-release gates.

A golden sample should not be merely the first unit that worked. It should be a characterized, stable reference with known hardware revision, firmware revision, calibration data, modal response, actuator properties, and acceptance results. Its purpose is to detect process drift and distinguish a product change from a test-system change.

The pilot should include time-separated builds and, where possible, more than one material or supplier lot. A process can look consistent when one engineer builds a small group of units under special attention. It must be tested under normal production staffing, tooling, inspection frequency, and takt time before release.

## 7. Production-phase management, testing, and performance consistency

### 7.1 Qualify suppliers and control incoming material

Supplier approval should examine process capability and change control, not only catalog specifications or a successful prototype sample. A piezoelectric factory should be able to show control from incoming ceramic through shipment, including:

- raw-material control;
- in-process inspection;
- final performance testing;
- nonconformance handling;
- batch traceability.

[The supplier-quality checklist](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality.html) recommends these five evidence areas and calls for strict engineering-change control over ceramics, adhesives, electrodes, wiring, and packaging.

Incoming inspection should be risk-based but functionally relevant. Depending on the component, it may include:

- ceramic lot and certificate verification;
- dimensions, flatness, and parallelism;
- capacitance, dielectric loss, and insulation;
- d33 or sampled electromechanical properties;
- actuator stroke, stiffness, resonance, or force;
- flexure geometry and surface condition;
- adhesive batch, shelf life, and storage;
- sensor gain, noise, and calibration status;
- amplifier PCB component and firmware revision.

A supplier sample that passes inspection does not demonstrate serial stability. The checklist warns that pilot units often receive extra care, while serial output exposes actual process capability. It recommends a pilot order with predefined gates for incoming quality, documentation, packaging, lead-time discipline, and functional consistency across multiple lots or time-separated shipments. [InduInsight’s supplier assessment](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/When_a_Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Becomes_a_Reliability_Risk.html) makes this prototype-to-serial distinction explicit.

### 7.2 Use standardized work and controlled fixtures

The production process should specify not only what to assemble but how to assemble it. Standardized work should define:

- cleaning and contamination limits;
- part orientation and datum sequence;
- fixture identification and setup verification;
- actuator seating and side-load limits;
- preload application and measurement;
- fastener type, torque, and sequence;
- adhesive dispensing and cure;
- sensor alignment and zeroing;
- cable routing and strain relief;
- electronics programming and configuration;
- environmental conditioning before calibration;
- retest and rework rules.

Fixtures should control the variables that are too sensitive to leave to operator judgment. A load cell or displacement-controlled preload station is preferable to relying only on screw torque when preload is a critical parameter. A laser or optical alignment gauge is preferable to visual centering when sensor-axis error materially affects cross-axis performance.

Tool wear should be monitored. Locating pins, nests, cutters, WEDM guides, dispensing needles, torque tools, and calibration references can all drift. The APQP worked example uses a shot counter to trigger locating-pin replacement at 100,000 cycles and an in-line laser sensor to measure a critical air gap. Its $`0.05\pm0.01\ \mathrm{mm}`$ air-gap example is for a micro-actuator line, not an isolator, but the prevention-and-detection logic transfers directly. [APQP process-control example](https://ansv.net/en/posts/apqp-rd-practice/).

### 7.3 Monitor process capability with SPC

Statistical process control should monitor both upstream variables and final functional outputs.

Upstream charts may include:

- flexure thickness and hinge dimensions;
- cavity length and parallelism;
- bond-line thickness;
- cure temperature and time;
- assembly preload;
- fastener torque;
- actuator capacitance and leakage;
- sensor offset and gain;
- amplifier output gain and current;
- firmware programming status.

Functional charts may include:

- actuator free stroke and stiffness;
- resonance frequency;
- hysteresis width;
- assembled modal frequencies;
- cross-axis coupling;
- sensor noise floor;
- closed-loop bandwidth;
- residual transmissibility;
- settling time;
- control effort.

X-bar/R or equivalent charts can detect changes in mean and within-subgroup variation. Individuals and moving-range charts may be appropriate when one unit per operation is available. Ppk is useful for long-term performance, but it should not replace Cpk from a stable short-term process. The control plan should define reaction limits, lot containment, investigation triggers, and restart criteria.

The APQP example specifies reactions such as stopping a line after one point beyond a $`3\sigma`$ zone, nine consecutive points on one side of the centerline, or six consecutive increases or decreases. These exact rules should be adapted to the actual process and risk, but they illustrate that an SPC chart must have a pre-agreed action, not merely a display.

Capability analysis must be performed on the actual product and production process. The reported micro-actuator example with $`C_{pk}=1.62`$ cannot be used to claim that a complete precision isolator has equivalent capability. The isolator’s relevant distributions must be measured after assembly, calibration, and final test.

### 7.4 Maintain serial-number genealogy

Every unit should have a serial-number record linking:

- ceramic and actuator lot;
- sensor and amplifier serial numbers;
- flexure and machined-part lots;
- adhesive batch and cure record;
- operators and assembly station;
- fixture and tool IDs;
- preload and alignment measurements;
- firmware and hardware revisions;
- calibration coefficients and date;
- end-of-line test data;
- environmental conditioning;
- nonconformances, rework, and concessions;
- field failures and corrective actions.

Traceability should be granular enough to distinguish a material-lot issue from an operator, fixture, supplier, or firmware issue. The supplier checklist recommends tracing each unit or lot back to materials, operators, tools, and test results so that failures can be isolated quickly. [InduInsight](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality.html) also emphasizes that deviations should be documented, contained, and permanently corrected.

Calibration data should be stored in a structured database rather than only printed on a certificate. The record should preserve raw measurements, fitted parameters, uncertainty, test conditions, software version, and acceptance decision. If a controller uses an individual actuator model, the firmware should verify that the correct calibration file is loaded for that serial number.

### 7.5 End-of-line acceptance testing

End-of-line testing should combine fast 100% screening with deeper sampled or periodic qualification.

A practical 100% screen can include:

- visual and dimensional inspection of critical interfaces;
- capacitance and dielectric-loss measurement;
- insulation resistance and leakage;
- amplifier voltage and current verification;
- actuator stroke or force at defined points;
- resonance or impedance check;
- preload and alignment;
- sensor zero, gain, and noise;
- short closed-loop response test;
- cross-axis or functional interlock check;
- firmware and calibration identification;
- protection and fault-response test.

A system-level acceptance test should include at least a low-amplitude frequency sweep or modal check, a defined disturbance or shaker test, residual motion measurement, and a step or load-disturbance response. The test should use the production payload or a controlled representative payload, defined cable routing, and known environmental conditions.

The supplier checklist recommends final checks for displacement, force, capacitance, resonance, hysteresis, insulation resistance, and response under specified drive conditions. It also recommends reliability screening for cycling, temperature exposure, humidity stress, and drift after storage or transport simulation. [InduInsight](https://www.induinsighthq.com/news/Precision_Fluid/Micro_Actuators/Piezoelectric_Actuator_Factory_Checklist_for_Stable_OEM_Quality) lists these as evidence of process maturity, but the exact limits and sampling plan must be set by the isolator’s requirements.

The test system itself requires calibration and Gage R&R. If a production laser, accelerometer, force sensor, or shaker has drifted, an apparent unit-to-unit shift may be a measurement-system shift. Reference units and check standards should be tested periodically to detect that condition.

### 7.6 Compare units and lots on common axes

Unit-to-unit consistency should not be judged by whether every unit has identical raw voltage or displacement. It should be judged by whether each unit meets the same functional metrics under the same test conditions.

Use a common test matrix:

- same payload mass and center of gravity;
- same cable and utility arrangement;
- same temperature and humidity;
- same sensor bandwidth and filtering;
- same actuator drive waveform;
- same preload;
- same disturbance spectrum;
- same controller and firmware revision;
- same measurement reference.

Compare:

- mean, standard deviation, range, and distribution shape;
- modal frequencies and damping;
- actuator gain and phase;
- sensor noise;
- cross-axis transfer;
- closed-loop transmissibility;
- residual acceleration or velocity;
- settling time;
- control effort;
- calibration drift.

Separate variation into:

- within-unit repeatability;
- operator or setup reproducibility;
- unit-to-unit variation;
- lot-to-lot variation;
- time or aging variation.

A unit with an unusual but passing result should not automatically be “tuned” into the population. The investigation should determine whether the result reflects a real product difference, an incorrect calibration file, a test setup error, or an emerging process trend.

### 7.7 Environmental qualification, fatigue, and aging

Environmental qualification should reproduce the actual service risks:

- temperature cycling and thermal gradients;
- high and low temperature operation;
- humidity exposure;
- storage and transport;
- mechanical shock and vibration;
- actuator cycling and fatigue;
- electrical overvoltage or repeated high-field operation;
- insulation and leakage after exposure;
- calibration drift after conditioning;
- modal stability after aging.

Tests should be performed at component, subassembly, and product level. For example, ceramic insulation may pass in isolation while a bonded stack fails after thermal cycling because of adhesive mismatch or electrode-edge stress. A flexure may survive static stress but drift after high-cycle operation. A controller may meet room-temperature performance but lose phase margin after a resonance shifts.

A manufacturer reports open-loop motion consistency after more than one billion cycles for one actuator family and a separate test article reaching $`3.22\times10^{12}`$ cycles. [The PI/TMC white paper](https://www.techmfg.com/learning/whitepapers/piezo-driven-active-vibration-control-pushes-limits) gives these results as manufacturer-specific endurance evidence, not as a universal lifetime for all piezoelectric actuators. Qualification should therefore use the actual ceramic, encapsulation, preload, drive waveform, environment, and duty cycle of the product.

Environmental tests should also be statistically connected to production. The product-specific evidence supplied here does not provide environmental or aging distributions across production lots for a complete isolation system. The appropriate production control is to define an initial qualification program, repeat it after significant changes, and use periodic sample testing or accelerated life monitoring to verify that production has not shifted.

### 7.8 Nonconformance, containment, and corrective action

A nonconformance process should distinguish:

- immediate containment of suspect units and lots;
- correction or rework;
- root-cause analysis;
- verification of the corrective action;
- disposition of already shipped units;
- update of PFMEA and control plan;
- supplier corrective action where appropriate;
- requalification after a process or design change.

Common failure patterns include:

- an actuator lot with shifted capacitance or resonance;
- preload outside the functional window;
- a sensor installed with incorrect orientation;
- an adhesive cure outside specification;
- a cable that bypasses a flexure;
- an amplifier component change that alters phase;
- a firmware or calibration-file mismatch;
- a test fixture that has worn or lost alignment;
- environmental drift mistaken for product drift.

The corrective-action record should retain the serial numbers, lot boundaries, measured data, containment decision, cause, action, and follow-up capability evidence. A closed corrective action should demonstrate that the relevant distribution returned to control, not merely that one failed unit was repaired.

## Closing judgment

A precision piezoelectric vibration isolator becomes accurate when its sensor, actuator, structure, electronics, and controller are designed as one measured plant. The highest-leverage improvements are usually a low-noise and correctly mounted sensing path, a stable high-voltage actuator interface, a stiff and thermally controlled structure with deliberately placed modes, measured preload and alignment, and a hybrid control architecture that combines feedback robustness with calibrated feedforward and nonlinear compensation.

Consistent products require a second layer of discipline. Requirements must be quantitative, tolerances must be allocated by sensitivity, designs must be verified at system level, and hardware, firmware, models, fixtures, and calibration records must remain under configuration control. In production, supplier and material control, standardized assembly, capable measurement systems, SPC, serial-number genealogy, product-specific calibration, end-of-line functional testing, environmental qualification, and closed corrective-action loops turn a successful prototype into a repeatable product.
